body.head: Theatrical Examiner
body.p:
If the Manager of the Lyceum continue to improve, as he has begun, in the selection of the new pieces offered him, his stage will soon outshine Covent-Garden in this respect, notwithstanding the great shew and still greater promises of that "classical" theatre. The comedy of Lost and Found, which was written, it seems, by a gentleman of the name of Masters, was unquestionably superior to the general run of our dramatic hacks; so is the farce of the Bee-Hive, in an inferior degree, though it turns out to have less originality than I thought;*—but by far the best step towards dramatic worthiness, that has been taken since Mr. Kenny’s World, has lately appeared in the new opera called the Peasant Boy. In general, the phrase "new opera," whether coming from the English or Italian theatre, implies something as old as it is foolish,—something altogether vulgar, tasteless, and mechanical,—in short, as mere a vehicle for music as a vagabond with a hand-organ on his back. To find therefore something decent on such an occasion, and not only decent, but something possessing a little novelty and more taste, is a refreshment, the gratefulness of which is only conceivable by the critics. The author tells us, in a modest and somewhat quaint advertisement, that his production is "founded upon a recorded fact in the Vienna Magazines for 1765," and that "in the fabrication of its scenes he hath had no further intent than to introduce upon the stage, though an unoffending medium, the music of one of our most meritorious national composers." He therefore begs to be "criticised rather comparatively than positively;" and as far as his interest is concerned, he is right;—but if a critic were to confine himself to comparison on such occasions, it is evident that the readers might have little or no idea of the author’s merits after all, since it is very possible, now-a-day’s, for a dramatist to be comparatively good, and at the same time to be positively bad.—The main story, though "a recorded fact," might easily be mistaken for a common stage plot. Baron Montaldi (Mr. Raymond) has a vehement inclination, common to younger brothers in romance, to be possessed of the fine estates of his elder brother the Duke Alberti (Mr. Holland) and finding no other way of succeeding, adopts the expedient, equally common, of dispatching the Duke in a bye-corner. The Duke, who is returning home from the wars, and the happiness of whose arrival is anticipated by his lady and household, is accordingly encountered in a dark wood by the Baron in disguise, who after leaving him for dead, flies from an unknown pursuer, and in order to baffle discovery, drops his disguise at the door of a cottage on the road. This disguise, together with a blood-stained dagger, is unluckily picked up by a peasant boy (Miss Kelly), who, unnerved at the sight, stands trembling with them in his hand, and is seized in this attitude by a party of soldiers, who have been sent after the assassin. The affair is brought before the Duke, who, in order to avoid being judge in his own case, seats his brother on the judgment-seat. The youth,—son of an old soldier and sustained by his conscious innocence,—strenuously, though with great agitation, denies the fact, but is nevertheless about to be sentenced to death by the perturbed villain on the bench, when, as a last resource, he calls upon the name of one Ludovico (Mr. Lovegrove), who had begged him so to do when in prison;—Ludovico comes forward, and to the astonishment of the persons present, the delight of the boy and his father, and the utter dismay of the judge, declares that when the attempt at assassination was made, he had pursued the man, given him a wound across the hand, and taken from his finger in the struggle an emerald ring;—it is recollected that Montaldi’s hand had latterly been wrapped in a bandage, and the Duchess also recollects, that she had presented him with an emerald ring in token of her esteem:—the Court starts up;—the Judge rushes down from the bench to demand the ring, and in the desperation of the moment, stabs himself;—and the piece concludes, as of old, with the happiness of two pair of lovers, the peasant and his mistress (Mrs. Bland) and a lady and gentleman (Miss Duncan and Mr. Phillips) whose courtings and coynesses had formed what is called the under-plot of the Opera. The latter part of this plot is interesting, as all trial incidents are, if decently managed; but there is nothing of what is new or surprising in it; and the characters, as far as regard themselves, are evidently so many nonentities. It is not in his story therefore, or in his observation of men and manners, that the author has excelled his contemporaries;—it is in his style of writing, in the manifest superiority of his habits of thinking and feeling, and in the air and turn of his poetry:—in a word, he is a man of taste, and Messrs. Dibdin and Reynolds are not; and this simple distinction throws an immeasurable distance between the author of the Peasant Boy, and the authors of the Cabinet and the Exiles. The language of the piece, generally speaking, is easy and well mannered; and the conduct of the scenes judicious, except in one instance, where the lady and gentleman above-mentioned are made to encounter each other with gay speeches, the very moment after the poor peasant had left their presence in order to be tried for his life. This may be a touch of the court, or a stroke of dramatic contrast; but then the author should not have violated great beauties for a less; the lovers are persons of virtue and sensibility, and as he evidently intended they should be thought so, he should have taken care to preserve their character.—The words of the songs are decidedly the best that have been heard for years, not excepting Mr. Cumberland’s later attempts in verse. Two or three of them, it is true, would not throw us into violent astonishment had they been written by Mr. Cherry;—the humourous one, in particular, respecting a marvellous well, the first draught of which decided the balance of power between new-married couples, is stale and badly told; but in general, the songs evince the taste of a man well acquainted with the poets, and perhaps not unlikely to become a poet of a lower order himself, if he is young and prepared to study. It is quite new, in a modern theatre, for a critic to hear songs about Petrarch, and to be reminded of some of the most pleasing productions of amatory poetry. The idea, at the commencement of the second act, of dismissing Love and recalling him, has often appeared in poetry, and has been particularly enlarged upon by Buchanan in the beautiful hendecasyllables beginning "Risus, blanditiæ, procacitates;"—the song of "Whither strays my lover," which Mr. Kelly has certainly set to a most graceful and fluent melody, is a delicate imitation of that exquisite little piece of Herrick’s, beginning "Their eyes the glow-worms lend thee"—but some of the other songs are not destitute of originality:—the following simile I do not recollect to have seen before:—
As AEtna convulsively clasps in her breast
A spirit she doubts whether evil or blest,
Now mantling with olives and vines the warm ground,
Now scattering perdition tremendously round:—
So it fares with the lover, so wayward his fate! In the present state of the drama, he who brings the least taste to the composition of a play, is a real acquisition to the cause of good letters, as he may gradually help to lead the public mind round to its proper tone in these matters. It is to be wished therefore, that when a new dramatist meets with encouragement from impartial observers, it will stimulate him, not to a renewal of his faults in the hope of escaping by what little is praiseworthy, but to a proper ambition for what is altogether praiseworthy in the hope of escaping from his faults. The Author of the new Opera for instance, writing as he does in some instances, ought not to have written as he does in others.

The new opera of the Knight of Snowdon, which was produced here on Tuesday night, is attributed to a number of different people, and among others to Mr. Reynolds. It seems indeed about the pitch of that Gentleman, being in a style somewhat more respectable than Mr. Dibdin’s productions, but without the least air of novelty, like the generality of Mr. Morton's. In a word, it is very shewy and very common-place, and is barely worth notice on account of its being taken from Mr. Scott’s last, well-known poem of the Lady of the Lake. The reader may easily suppose, that what has been taken from this poem is infinitely the better part of it; yet, though dramatized from a Poet sufficiently theatrical in his subjects, it has little interest; and the best parts of the original must naturally have been lost to the imitator, inasmuch as they consist of description. The pitch of the Author’s mind is indeed sufficiently explained by his going to such a source for his ideas. It is purely borrowing at second-hand, and from a writer of second-rate genius. Mr. Scott is the feast of his day, as Darwin was of his; but it is a feast of cloying sweets, at which "crude surfeit reigns;" and the admirers of terse writing and pure invention are very much mistaken, if ten or twelve years do not drive the gorgeous knights and ladies of Mr. Scott as completely off the stage, as they have driven the enamoured pinks and gilly-flowers of the Doctor.
